clinical_knowledge.topic: Decompensated Alcohol-Related Liver Cirrhosis with Ascites evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Decompensated Alcohol-Related Liver Cirrhosis with Ascites is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis with IV albumin replacement if large volume, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: swollen abdomen and yellowing of the eyes over the past month

Key HPI features: 4-week progressive abdominal distension with ankle swelling and mild scleral icterus. Reports early satiety due to abdominal tightness, dark tea-coloured urine, and easy bruising. Denies haematemesis, melaena, or acute confusion, though spouse notes mild sleep disturbances.

Objective/Exam findings: Check vitals, weight, abdominal girth. Examine for stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, caput medusae, shifting dullness, asterixis). Bloods: LFTs, INR/PT, albumin, FBC, U&Es. Diagnostic paracentesis (SAAG, cell count to rule out SBP).
Relevant background/PMH: alcohol use disorder (heavy drinking 80g/day for 25 years, abstinent for past 4 months), hypertension
Current medications: thiamine 100mg OD, spironolactone 100mg OD (started recently by GP)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Decompensated Alcohol-Related Liver Cirrhosis with Ascites.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Confusion or drowsiness — suggests hepatic encephalopathy.
management_principles: Diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis with IV albumin replacement if large volume
Initiate lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy prophylaxis
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 57M with history of alcohol dependence presents with progressive ascites, peripheral oedema, jaundice, and sleep reversal over 4 weeks. No GI bleeding reported.
reference_soap.objective: Check vitals, weight, abdominal girth. Examine for stigmata of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia, caput medusae, shifting dullness, asterixis). Bloods: LFTs, INR/PT, albumin, FBC, U&Es. Diagnostic paracentesis (SAAG, cell count to rule out SBP).
reference_soap.assessment: Decompensated alcohol-related liver cirrhosis with ascites and mild hepatic encephalopathy. DDx: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression, portal vein thrombosis.
reference_soap.plan: Diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis with IV albumin replacement if large volume. Optimize diuretics (spironolactone + furosemide ratio). Initiate lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy prophylaxis. Ultrasound abdomen with Doppler and alpha-fetoprotein to screen for HCC. Hepatology referral.

learning_objectives: Elicit a detailed alcohol history quantified in units/grams and assess duration of abstinence
Screen systematically for complications of cirrhosis: ascites, variceal bleed risk, hepatic encephalopathy, SBP
Explain the rationale behind sodium restriction, diuretic therapy, and paracentesis
Provide compassionate communication surrounding liver disease prognosis and relapse prevention

teaching.diagnosis: Decompensated Alcohol-Related Liver Cirrhosis with Ascites
teaching.one_liner: Years of heavy drinking have scarred the liver; it can no longer make enough protein or clear fluid, so fluid pools in the abdomen and legs and the skin turns yellow.
red_flags: Confusion or drowsiness — suggests hepatic encephalopathy

must_ask.say: When did your belly start to swell, and has it been getting bigger?
How much alcohol were you drinking, and when did you last have a drink?
Has anyone noticed you seeming confused, forgetful, or sleeping differently?
Have you noticed your skin or eyes turning yellow, or your urine getting darker?
Have you noticed bruising more easily than before?
Does the swelling make it hard to breathe or lie flat?
Are you taking your water tablets exactly as prescribed?
